text: You have n balloons with numbers in nums. Bursting balloon i gives you nums of i minus one, times nums of i, times nums of i plus one coins; out-of-bounds neighbours count as one. After a burst, the neighbours become adjacent. Maximize the total coins.

Thanks. Before I dive in, I'd like to clarify a few things. Just to make sure I'm understanding this correctly — the coins for a burst depend on the current neighbours, which change as balloons pop, so the order is what I'm optimizing. And an edge balloon uses one for the missing side?
Exactly. Order is everything, and yes — treat missing sides as one. n goes up to three hundred.

Let me run through the example. Three, one, five, eight gives one hundred sixty-seven. If I greedily burst the biggest first, the eight pays five times eight times one, forty, and that greedy order ends at just forty-nine. The eight is worth more kept around as a neighbour, multiplying everything burst next to it. So greedy fails; the interaction between neighbours is the whole difficulty.

Hmm, let me think about this for a second. A naive approach would try every burst order, which is n factorial. The natural instinct is to pick which balloon to burst first and recurse — but that breaks. When I burst balloon k first, its left and right neighbours become adjacent, so the two halves merge and I can't split into independent subproblems. This problem reminds me of interval DP, where you split a range at a pivot. The fix is to reverse the question: which balloon bursts last? If k is the last to pop in some range, everything else in that range is already gone, so its neighbours are exactly the range's two boundaries. That coin value is fixed. And because k survived the whole time, it acted as a wall splitting the range into two halves that never interfered.

I'll pad nums with a one on each end, so every balloon has neighbours and there's no boundary special-casing. Then I use an open interval: dp of i, j is the max coins from bursting every balloon strictly between i and j — i and j themselves are not burst; they're the walls. dp of i, j is the max over k between them of dp of i, k plus dp of k, j plus nums of i times nums of k times nums of j. The open interval makes the split seamless: k is the right wall of the left piece and the left wall of the right piece at the same time, so the two pieces tile the range exactly. The answer is dp of zero, n plus one.

Here's the plan. dp of i, k and dp of k, j are both shorter intervals, so I fill by interval length, ascending — same discipline as any interval DP. One: pad nums with a one at each end. Two: for each length L from one to n, for each left wall i, set j to i plus L plus one and try every k in between. Three: return dp of zero, n plus one. Does this approach sound good, or would you rather I think of another way?

Alright, let me code this up. After padding, the indices run from zero to n plus one. The outer loop is L, the number of balloons inside the open interval; the middle loop is the left wall i; the inner loop is k, the last balloon to burst. One thing worth flagging — j equals i plus L plus one, not i plus L, because the two walls each take an index on top of the L balloons inside. Get that off by one and dp of zero, n plus one never gets filled. That's order n cubed time — n squared intervals times an order n choice of k — and order n squared space.
Why is the coin term nums of i times nums of k times nums of j, and not nums of k minus one times nums of k times nums of k plus one?

Because k is the last to go in this range, so its original neighbours, k minus one and k plus one, are already burst by then. The balloons still standing next to it are the range's untouched walls, i and j. That's precisely why the value is fixed and can serve as a DP transition — i and j never burst within this subproblem, so they're stable anchors. Using k minus one and k plus one would be the current-neighbours thinking that this whole reframe exists to escape.

Let's dry-run three, one, five, eight; padded, it's one, three, one, five, eight, one, and I compute dp of zero, five by trying each last balloon; expected one hundred sixty-seven. The row that wins is k equals four, the eight: the left piece, bursting three, one, five first, is worth one hundred fifty-nine, the right piece is empty, and the eight then pops between the two sentinel ones for eight more — one sixty-seven. That matches. Corner cases: one, five gives ten. A single balloon gives itself.

Let me think about complexity here. Time is order n cubed, space order n squared. Compared to brute force over all n factorial orders, reversing the question — first to last — turned factorial into cubic. Oh, one more thing — the same skeleton works as a memoized recursion top-down, which some find more intuitive, since you write it straight from the last-balloon definition. And it's worth noting why this problem is hard at all: the coins are a product of neighbours, so keeping a big balloon around as a neighbour pays off non-linearly. That's exactly what defeats greedy and forces a real search over orders.

Excellent. Three things stood out. You diagnosed exactly why burst first fails — the halves merge — and flipped to burst last so they stay independent. You justified the fixed coin term via the surviving walls. And the padding plus open interval design was clean. That's a strong answer to a hard problem — strong hire.
